cast.name: DAVID
cast.who: White, wealthy, two parents at home. The new library wing has his last name over the door.
tags: Family name over the library door

cast.name: ALEJANDRA
cast.who: Colombian, wealthy family, enormous performance pressure.
tags: Endometriosis — diagnosed in one year, managed on a schedule

cast.name: PRIYA
cast.who: Indian-American, wealthy immigrant family, heavy parental expectation.

cast.name: MEI
cast.who: Chinese-American, both parents doctors, a schedule with no air in it.

cast.name: REBECCA
cast.who: Ashkenazi Jewish, pediatrician mom, math-teacher dad. The house simply works.
tags: Two parents, both home by six
Homework help at the dinner table

cast.name: DANIEL

tags: Dad and two uncles run the business

cast.name: AYESHA
cast.who: Black. Her mother is the principal. They live across the street from the school, and half her homework has been done in the front office.
tags: A desk in the office when she needs one
Every teacher knows her name first

cast.name: GRACE

tags: A credit card for emergencies, used for dinners

cast.name: CARLOS

tags: Shares one car with three adults

tags: No internet past the county line

cast.name: ISABELLA

cast.name: FATIMA

tags: Gets two siblings out the door first

cast.name: RAJESH

tags: Mom is out the door at 5:30
Gets his sister to school first

cast.name: LING

cast.name: JAMAL

PE uniform stops two sizes short

A gym excuse in his own handwriting
Walks past the counselor's door daily

tags: Mom works overnights, sleeps at 8 AM
Kreyol at home, English everywhere else
Sister Yvette drives the church van

Translates the doctor, the landlord, the school

Called a terrorist in the lunch line

1.name: MORNING IN THE VILLAGE — GET TO SCHOOL
1.kaia: It's 7 AM. First bell is at 8:30. Everybody in this room has to get to the same building. Nobody starts from the same place.

2.name: AFTERNOON & EVENING — GET HOME
2.kaia: Last bell. Everyone goes home now — to whatever home is. Four hours until sleep, and the homework is due either way.

3.name: THE NIGHT — MAKE IT TO TOMORROW
3.kaia: Lights out in the village. Some of you get eight hours. Some of you get the kind of night you don't tell anyone about.

ayesha.sit: Your mom unlocks the building at 7:00. First bell is 8:30, and school is one crosswalk away — from your bedroom window you can read the marquee. The only question is when to cross.

auto.say: The building at 7:00 is dark, quiet, and briefly yours. You take the chair that spins in the front office, and at 8:00 the announcements come over the PA in the same voice that just told you to grab a jacket.
One crosswalk, about forty seconds. The guard holds the door open and asks after your mom, whom he already let in at seven.
You watch the first buses unload from the kitchen window, waffle in hand. You cross at 8:24 and are in your seat with five minutes to spare.

grace.sit: 7:35. Your mother left for the hospital before you were awake; your father never came home from his. School is four miles away, and how you get there is, as always, yours to figure out.

auto.say: The pin drops on the building across the street and you watch the driver's arrow circle it twice. You walk in at 8:41, rattled; nobody knew you were late until you mentioned it at lunch.

standard.say: The driver misses the turn for the school and does not slow down. You say stop twice before he does. You get out at a light eleven blocks away and walk the rest with your phone in your hand.

unsparing.say: The driver misses the turn and does not slow down, and the door does not open the first time you try it. You say stop three times, and the third one comes out in a voice you did not know you had. The neighborhood you get out into is one your parents chose for its safety. You walk eleven blocks through it with your phone unlocked in your hand. The money bought the phone and the safe neighborhood. It could not buy the ride going right.

auto.say: Back in September you taught yourself this route off a screenshot — the 14, the transfer at Croft, the 9. You're at the gate by 8:20 with a croissant from the place by the second stop.

choices.t: Text your dad for a ride

auto.say: You send it at 7:36, give it ten minutes, and take the bus anyway. At 11:52 he replies from between surgeries — “Leaving now?” — and by then you have been at school for three hours.

tyler.sit: Last night was a bad one. Your left arm has a mark you didn't have yesterday, and the kitchen is silent in the way that means he's still asleep. First bell is 8:30.

auto.say: The side door gets you to your seat at 8:27 and nobody looks twice. By third period the radiators are still on, and you take notes with your cuffs pinned under your palms.

She closes the door, photographs your arm twice, and asks her questions in a voice that has done this before. By noon there is a case number and an adult whose job is you; by last bell there is a voicemail at the house, and you know what time he gets home.

You sit behind the gas station with a bag of their ice until your arm will go through a sleeve without help. You slide in at 9:22, and the unexcused mark posts before lunch, next to two others from this year.

marie.sit: Your mom's key turns at 7:25, twelve hours after it turned the other way. Asleep by eight or sick by Friday — those are her words. Sister Yvette's van comes up the block at 7:40. First bell is 8:30.

auto.say: Sister Yvette pulls up at 7:40 with four kids in and the choir tape on low. You're at the gate by 8:20 with somebody's harmony stuck in your head.
You carry your shoes to the mat and ease the door to behind you. Twenty-five minutes, a banana eaten walking, and the light under her door was off before you hit the stairs.
She's up before you finish asking, keys in hand, coat over her scrubs. You're at the curb by 8:15, and she'll pay for those twenty minutes at 3 AM on somebody else's stairs.

rebecca.sit: Your mom leaves for the clinic at 7:30 and can drop you early. Your dad leaves at 8:05 and passes the school door at 8:25. Both offers stand every morning. First bell is 8:30.

pass.say: The library at 7:50 is empty, warm, and yours. The homework is checked twice before the first bus even pulls in.

fail.say: You second-guess question four into the wrong answer. Your dad teaches math; it takes four minutes tonight, somewhere between the soup and the salad.

choices.t: Ride with dad, exactly on time

auto.say: He pulls up at 8:25 like a train arriving. You spend the five spare minutes on the steps with Hannah and walk in mid-sentence.
Twelve minutes of flat streets with a granola bar in your pocket. Both parents wave from the porch like you're leaving for a month.

daniel.sit: Dad can drive you. Uncle Davoud's van passes the school anyway, full of cousins. Grandma has already called twice, offering to walk you. The only question this morning is who gets to.

auto.say: He takes the long way to finish the argument about offside. You're at the curb by 8:10, mid-sentence, and he's still wrong.
She hands you a foil package at the gate: tahdig, still warm from this morning. By noon, three people have offered to trade.

choices.cost: The front seat goes by age.

auto.say: Uncle Davoud's van, four cousins, one loud vote about tonight's cake. You get out at the gate still laughing.

mei.sit: Your parents booked a 7:30 AP-chem review session on the way to school. You found out at 6:50, when your mother handed you the packet in the car. First bell is 8:30.

choices.t: Do the review in the car

pass.say: Both right. You are dropped at the curb at 8:14, on schedule and already tired.

fail.say: One wrong, at a red light, with your mother watching. Nothing is said, and you spend first period redoing that question in your head.

auto.say: She says "of course" and turns the radio off. It is not mentioned again, which is how you know it was recorded.
They agree immediately, because it is a reasonable request and you are a reasonable daughter. The Tuesday session is now twice as long.

fatima.sit: Your mom's shift started at 6 and she left before anyone was up. You ate before dawn; the little ones haven't eaten at all. Their school is eight blocks in the wrong direction.

auto.say: Eggs, toast, two zipped backpacks. At 8:40 the guard holds your ID up twice before waving you in, and the tardy goes next to your name.
All three of you make the bell. At 10:15 your brother's teacher writes “unfocused” in the folder that follows him to every meeting.

choices.t: Call your mom at the hospital
choices.cost: A phone she isn't allowed to touch.

auto.say: She whispers you through it: granola bars behind the rice, two dollars in the drawer. All three of you make the bell. A charge nurse saw the phone, and dinner tonight is quiet in a new way.

rajesh.sit: Your mom left for the hospital at 5:30. Your sister is eight and will not get out of bed. Her school opens at 7:50. Yours is twenty minutes the other way.

choices.t: Get her up, fed, dressed, and there

auto.say: Cereal, shoes, the fight about the shoes. Her door at 7:50, yours at 8:28, and first period spent keeping your eyes open on purpose.

choices.t: Leave her with the neighbor in 4B

auto.say: She says yes before you finish the question. You are on time, and you spend all six periods on what you actually know about her: a name, an apartment number.

standard.say: The woman in 4B steps out at 9:15 and does not come back. The school calls about your sister's absence, and the hospital calls your mother off the ward. The front office pulls you out of second period to go and get your sister. She has spent three hours alone in a stranger's apartment, sitting where she could see the door.

unsparing.say: The woman in 4B steps out, and your sister waits twenty minutes, then goes looking for you in the direction she thinks your school is. A man at the transit stop notices an eight-year-old alone at ten in the morning, a stranger who could have been anyone. This time, he calls the school.

choices.cost: The call to the nursing station.

auto.say: You are in your seat on time. At 10:40 her school calls your mom's floor, and tonight is decided before lunch.

ling.sit: Your mom got home at 11:40 last night. The landlord calls at 7:30 about the lease renewal, in English. First bell is 8:30, twenty-five minutes away on foot.

choices.t: Sit at the table and translate the call

pass.say: Rent, deposit, renewal date, all of it lands in both languages. You walk into first period at 8:45, marked tardy.

fail.say: A line about "prevailing market rate" goes past too fast to carry across. Your mom says yes to it anyway, and you spend six periods turning the phrase over.

choices.cost: Your mom, alone on the phone.

auto.say: You make first bell. At lunch she texts a photo of the page she signed and asks what "arbitration" means.

choices.t: Ask the landlord to call back at 4

auto.say: He says fine in a way that means it isn't. You're on time, and you spend the whole day rehearsing the call in your head.

jamal.sit: Suhoor has to happen before Fajr at 6:15, and after that there is nothing until sunset. Your dad's shift started at five; your mom's doesn't end until seven. The bus is at 7:25.

choices.cost: Nothing until sunset, on no food since last night.

auto.say: You make the prayer and you make the bus. By second period the whiteboard is just shapes, and sunset is nine hours away.

choices.cost: The first prayer of five, and the only meal until dark.

auto.say: Sleep wins until seven. You make the bus with your eyes half open, and spend first period deciding you'll make it all up later, and second period, and third.
Eggs at 5:35, prayer at 6:15, bus at 7:25. You wait outside the locked doors until the building decides to open, and by last period you've read the same paragraph four times.

aisha.sit: Mom left for inventory at 5:40. Getting dressed means finding what fits, what covers, and what the hallway won't have something to say about. The bus is at 7:52.

choices.t: Take the time to get it right

auto.say: You walk in at 8:40 feeling like yourself. The office writes down the tardy without looking up.

choices.cost: Feeling wrong until the last bell.

auto.say: 7:52, and you're on it, in the first thing your hands touch. You spend all six periods tugging at the hem.

choices.t: Leave the scarf on the hook
choices.cost: One day of being someone else.

auto.say: The hallway has nothing to say for once. You catch your reflection in the trophy case between classes and look away.

kavi.sit: Breakfast at 7. Your mother uses the old name twice before the toast is done. The pin with your pronouns is in your jacket pocket, where it lives until the bus stop.

choices.t: Change at the bus stop, same as always

auto.say: You pin it on once the house is out of sight and are Kavi by first bell. On time, in your seat, faster at the changeover every week.
Your father goes quiet. Your mother says something about layoffs, then “focus on your studies,” and drives you to school so you won't be late. The name goes unsaid. Either one.
All morning you answer to anything and correct no one. It is the smoothest morning in weeks. Neither building says a word to Kavi, which was the plan.

amina.sit: Grandma rides the bus with you since the comments started. This morning her hip is bad and she is moving slowly. The bus comes in ten minutes. The next one is half an hour later.

choices.t: Help her get ready, take the next bus

auto.say: You get her ready and take the 8:10 together. She watches every face that gets on. You walk in at 8:46 and the office writes it down.
Alone on the 7:40, you make first bell. All day you do the math on how she gets down the stairs by herself.

choices.cost: Rushing an old woman down the stairs.

auto.say: Both of you make the 7:40. She took the stairs too fast and pays for it at every stop. She says nothing about being hurried, in either language.
Heating pad against her hip, you stay. She apologizes all morning. When the attendance letter comes, you will be the one who translates it.

david.sit: Your parents can drive you. They also want to drop your brother at soccer first. First bell is 8:30.

choices.t: Ask them to skip the soccer drop-off
choices.cost: Your brother sulks. That is the entire cost.

pass.say: You are in your seat by 8:20 with your homework done in the car.

fail.say: On the second question, you blank. Nobody writes anything down; nobody ever has.

choices.t: Ride along and walk in five minutes late

auto.say: The office waves you through without looking up. No tardy is recorded.
Soccer, then school, then a bagel. You arrive early enough to be bored.

alejandra.sit: The driver leaves at 7:15. Your mother wants last night's AP chem lab reviewed in the car. Your hands are shaking.

choices.t: Review the lab in the car

pass.say: Both correct. She nods once and goes back to her phone. You are on time.

fail.say: One wrong. She says nothing the rest of the ride. You are present and already behind in your own head.

choices.t: Tell her you'll do it at lunch

auto.say: You arrive rested. Your phone buzzes nine times before first period.
The lab is perfect. You are in school, shaking, running on nothing.

priya.sit: A district letter needs translating for your parents before you leave. Your tutor wants last night's problem set checked. You have 25 minutes.

choices.t: Translate the letter, skip the set
choices.cost: Your tutor reports it to your father.

pass.say: Your parents understand the deadline. You are on time and quietly proud.

fail.say: You miss a line about the signature. Your father signs nothing. You are in school, worrying.

choices.t: Do the set, leave the letter on the counter

auto.say: The set is flawless. The letter sits unread until Friday. Something lapses that nobody explains to you.
All of it gets done. You are in school, on time, and cannot keep your eyes open.

carlos.sit: You open the shop at 6. Your dad's shift ended at 5:30 and the car isn't back. School is 40 minutes on foot.

choices.t: Wait ten minutes for the car, close out the register

pass.say: The drawer balances, the car pulls in, you slide into second period. Tardy #4 this month.

fail.say: Short drawer. You leave anyway. Tardy #4, and you'll hear about the register tonight.

choices.cost: The shop loses the morning rush.

auto.say: You walk in at 9:05. Tardy. Your mother finds the shop closed and understands exactly why.

choices.t: Stay until your dad is back

auto.say: He gets back at 10:40. There is no point going in now.

chase.sit: The route bus is 70 minutes, if it runs. Your dad took the truck last night and hasn't come back.

choices.t: Take the route bus and read on the way

pass.say: You finish the reading somewhere past the second cattle gate. You make first bell.

fail.say: An incident on the tracks holds the bus at the crossing for twenty minutes; nobody at school asks what kind. You walk in late with nothing prepared.

choices.t: Ask your grandmother's neighbor for a ride

auto.say: He drops you at the flagpole at 8:12 and won't take gas money. You are in.

standard.say: The neighbor's truck dies on the shoulder eleven miles out, and it is two hours before anything else comes down the road. You get to school at noon with your hands too cold to sign the late sheet. Nobody at either end had noticed you were missing.

unsparing.say: Black ice, on the curve the county doesn't sand. The seat in third period stays empty, and after a week the teacher stops setting handouts on it. The route bus passes the spot twice a day, and for a while the driver slows down there, and then he doesn't.

choices.t: Go look for the truck first

auto.say: By 11 AM you have found the truck. Your dad is not with it.

isabella.sit: Bad pain day. You can barely stand upright. Your mom already left; she cannot miss another shift.

choices.t: Go anyway and try to get someone to believe you
choices.cost: The whole day, spent on staying upright.

pass.say: You name every symptom clearly. The nurse writes “cramps” and sends you back to class. You stay, in pain, all day.

fail.say: Words won't come out fast enough. The nurse suggests losing weight. You go back to class.

auto.say: You lie on the bathroom floor until 2 PM. The absence is marked unexcused.
“This is likely weight-related. Try walking more.” You go in late with nothing.

marcus.sit: You and three younger siblings. $2.50 for fares that cost $3 each. The youngest won't put his shoes on.

choices.t: All take the bus; one of you stays home

pass.say: You get three of you there by 8:50. Your youngest is home alone with a plan and a phone number.

fail.say: You can't name a single place to send him. You take everyone back inside.

choices.t: Walk it. Ninety minutes. Everyone late.

pass.say: Four of you walk in at 9:20. Four tardies. Everyone is in a building.

fail.say: The youngest sits down in the road at minute forty and will not get up.

standard.say: The light changes while the youngest is still in the street, and a car stops an arm's length short of him. You carry him the rest of the way, and nobody in this family goes anywhere today.

unsparing.say: The light changes while the youngest is still in the street. The forms ask for a parent or guardian, and there is a long pause at every counter while someone decides what to do with you. At the elementary school across town, a teacher empties a cubby into a grocery bag.

choices.cost: A risk you cannot take back.

auto.say: You get to school at 8:35. You check your phone eleven times before lunch.
You keep all four of them safe and none of you sees a classroom.

lucia.sit: Your mom did not come home from her night shift. Your siblings are 6, 8 and 10. No money, no adult you are allowed to call.
lucia.note: There is no challenge here. There is nothing to win.

choices.t: Go to school and leave them

auto.say: You get to the corner and turn around. You cannot make your feet do it.
You make cereal, lock the door, and count the hours. Everyone is safe. Nobody is in school.
You don't know which facility. You don't have anyone you can ask. You come home at noon with nothing.

jayson.sit: You didn't sleep. The roster still has your old name on it. Two siblings need walking to the elementary door.

choices.cost: Being called the wrong name for six hours.

auto.say: Both siblings are in by 8:15. You sit through attendance being read wrong and say nothing.
You get them to the door, then go back and sleep until three.

choices.t: Ask the front office for help

auto.say: The counselor covers four schools. Next opening: three weeks. You are marked present. Nothing else changes.

sophia.sit: Your mom hasn't left her room in nine days. If anyone finds out, you and your brother get separated.

choices.t: Get your brother in, go in, say nothing

pass.say: You give the right answers to every question. Not one teacher looks twice. You are in school and completely alone in it.

fail.say: One question about a permission slip, and you freeze. The teacher walks you to the office. The day goes elsewhere.

choices.t: Stay home and keep her drinking water

auto.say: Three sips is all she'll take. School marks you absent and asks nothing else.

choices.cost: The thing you are most afraid of.

auto.say: A report is filed within the hour. You spend the day in an office, not a classroom.

ayesha.sit: Last bell at 3:10. Your mom has meetings until five, and the front office keeps a desk for you by the mail cubbies. Home is one crosswalk away, whenever you're ready.

choices.cost: The walk home in the dark, all eighty feet of it.

auto.say: Homework at your desk while the secretaries pass the pretzel jar down. The essay prints double-sided on the office printer, and when the stapler jams, three adults come over to fix it.
The crossing guard stops traffic for you at 3:15. You work at the kitchen table, where you can see the light in your mom's office window, and at 5:20 you watch her cross the street toward dinner.

choices.cost: An hour of homework, moved to after dinner.

auto.say: You sort district mail into the teacher cubbies and learn the building by box: who gets the catalogs, who gets the attendance letters. The head secretary pays you from the butterscotch jar and calls you her best hire.

grace.sit: 3:40, and the apartment is exactly as you left it, because nobody else has been in it. There's an essay due Friday, a fridge holding sparkling water and half a lime, and a card that covers whatever the fridge doesn't.

choices.cost: An hour and a recipe video.

auto.say: The pan catches at step four, and the building alarm empties all six floors into the parking lot, you still in the oven mitts. The fine posts to your parents' card and is paid the way everything is paid — without anyone asking what burned.
By now the driver knows the building code. You eat at the island with a video propped against the fruit bowl no adult has been home to refill.
You write for five careful hours alone with the prompt. At 11:05 you check the rubric — compare, not argue — five pages in the wrong direction.

tyler.sit: 3:10. From the corner you can read the driveway: the truck is home early, nose-in, and the kitchen light is off. You have been reading this driveway since you were nine, and today it isn't saying.

choices.t: Go in now, while it's quiet

auto.say: The side door, socks on the stairs. He's asleep in the recliner with the TV going, and you eat cereal standing at the counter and do homework with your door cracked so you can hear.

choices.cost: Five hours of not knowing what you're walking into.

auto.say: You do every assignment at the table by the radiator and check the driveway from across the street at 8:40. The truck is gone, the kitchen light is on, and your mother has saved you a plate without saying anything about the time.

Jake's mom sets a fourth plate and refills it before you can ask, which is its own kind of question. She asks twice, lightly, whether anyone knows where you are, and at 9:40 you let yourself into a house where someone does.

marie.sit: The hall behind the church opens at 3:30. Long tables, a box of sharpened pencils, Tati Rose reading homework like a lease. Around six, dinner plates appear without being announced. The hall closes at seven.

auto.say: Tati Rose is nobody's actual aunt, which has never once stopped her. Your essay goes home two sentences shorter and better for it.

choices.t: Stay for a plate and the van

auto.say: A plate lands in front of you at six: diri kole, a chicken leg, sos pwa from somebody's mother's pot. Sister Yvette drops you home in time to catch your mom before she leaves, bag packed, ten minutes to spare.

choices.t: Stay till the chairs are stacked

auto.say: You hold the door for the coffee urn and Sister Yvette locks up at 7:10. Home has all the quiet the hall doesn't, and the envelope on the counter stays face-down, unopened while you're in the room.

rebecca.sit: Home by 3:30. Homework, youth group at seven, the new episode at nine. Four free hours. The only question is the order.

auto.say: Done by eight at the kitchen table, your dad drifting past to admire your margins. You watch the episode with popcorn and nothing hanging over it.
On the drive home your dad quizzes you on the problem set at red lights, which he thinks is a game and which, annoyingly, works. The homework is done before the opening credits.
Homework by 6:40, youth group at seven, home for the opening credits. Your mom has saved you the good end of the couch.

daniel.sit: School lets out at 3:10. The shop could use an hour of shelving and your dad pays family wages. Grandma's table is cleared for homework by 3:30. Nobody needs you anywhere; everybody wants you somewhere.

choices.t: An hour at the shop first

auto.say: You shelve saffron and cardamom and Uncle Farhad rounds your pay up to a ten. Homework at grandma's by 4:40, next to a plate of peeled cucumbers.
Homework is done by five, next to a tea you didn't ask for. The cousins land at 5:30, straight from Hebrew school, and the table becomes a FIFA bracket.
Uncle Davoud checks your math between customers, once wrong on purpose to see if you catch it. You catch it.

mei.sit: Tutor at 4:30, piano at 6, homework after. The grade portal updates at 9 PM. Your parents refresh it at 9:01.

auto.say: Tutor, piano, three assignments, lights out at 12:40. The portal shows a perfect evening. There is no field for the rest of it.

choices.t: Tell your parents it's too much

auto.say: Your father says, "We do this for your future." Your mother agrees. Tomorrow's schedule is identical to today's.
It works for six days, until the studio calls your mother to confirm the cancellation. Dinner that night has one topic.

fatima.sit: Home by four with both of them. You are fasting; iftar is at 7:52. They are seven and nine and hungry now, and your English essay is due at midnight.

auto.say: Rice and chicken by five, standing over a pan you can't touch. You sit down to the essay at six with nothing in you, and the title is still all there is when the light starts to go.

choices.cost: An hour of them getting louder.

auto.say: You get four sentences down before the fighting starts in the next room. At 5:40 you close the laptop and cook, which is how this was always going to go.
Essay propped against the flour jar, you stir. Dinner is late, the essay is 400 words of filler, and sundown is still two hours away.

rajesh.sit: Home at 4:30, both of you. She has a worksheet she can't start. You have three assignments you haven't. Your mom is home at seven, on her feet since six.

pass.say: Seven times eight, which word is the noun. She gets it, mostly. Your own three start at 9:15 and two of them finish.

fail.say: You explain it three different ways and she cries at the third. The worksheet goes back in her folder half-blank, and yours never leaves the bag.

auto.say: All three of yours get done. She gives up at the second question and watches cartoons until seven, the worksheet face-down on the couch.

choices.t: Snack first, then split the time

auto.say: Toast at 4:45, then thirty minutes each. Both end up half-done, and when your mom asks how homework went, you both say fine.

ling.sit: You let yourself in at 4:30. Eight envelopes on the counter, all in English. Your mom is at the restaurant until 11 and two assignments are due tomorrow. You start the rice first.

auto.say: The fourth envelope is a shut-off notice dated Thursday. You catch it in time to set up a payment plan, and both assignments stay in the backpack.

choices.t: Homework first, mail on the weekend

auto.say: Both assignments are done and turned in. The overdue bill surfaces three days later under a takeout menu, with a $45 late fee attached.

choices.t: Skim the stack, do the shortest assignment

auto.say: You handle the envelope stamped URGENT and the worksheet due first period. The essay and five unopened letters move to tomorrow, which is already full.

jamal.sit: Asr falls at 4:15, right in the middle of math tutoring. The school has no prayer space; it has never needed one before. Tutoring is what's keeping your grade above a C.

auto.say: The quadratics finally click. You keep the count in the back of your planner, on a page no teacher will ever ask to see.
You make Asr on a folded hoodie between the second and third floor and get back for the last twenty minutes. By last bell the video is up, and somebody has added a sound effect.

choices.t: Ask the front office for a room
choices.cost: A meeting instead of the prayer.

auto.say: For the whole eleven minutes the vice principal is kind about it, and writes herself a note. There is an empty conference room by the gym, and no one who can find the key.

aisha.sit: PE, fourth period. The uniform comes in five sizes and stops two before yours. The weigh-in happens by the open gym door. The comments cover your body, your scarf, and your skin, sometimes in the same sentence.

choices.cost: The mile, in front of everyone.

auto.say: You run the mile in a uniform held closed with a safety pin. The teacher hears the third comment and finds something on his clipboard to read.
Fourth period goes by behind the last shelf in the library. The cut posts to the system before you're back in fifth; the zero posts Friday.

choices.cost: Being the one with the complaint.

auto.say: Calmly, with dates, you name all of it. The vice principal says “kids will be kids” and asks, before you go, whether the scarf comes off for gym.

kavi.sit: Four people on your father's team were laid off Friday. The new rule arrives by group text: straight home, grades only, no clubs. The QSA meets today at 3:30. It is the one hour a week you spend under one name.

auto.say: You're home by 3:50 with your homework spread out where it can be seen. The grades are safe. At 4:30 your phone starts filling with photos of a meeting happening without you.

choices.t: Go, and call it a study group
choices.cost: A second story to keep up.

auto.say: For one hour you are only Kavi, arguing about fonts on the bake sale poster. On the bus home you text “study group ran long.” Your mother sends back a thumbs up.

choices.t: Ask permission and leave out why
choices.cost: Making the case without the reason.

auto.say: You text your mother at lunch and keep it vague: a club, an hour, good for college. “Clubs are distractions right now.” The one reason that might have changed her mind is the one you can't type.

amina.sit: Home at 4. Grandma's hip is worse and the clinic line closes at five. Somebody has to make the call in English, and there is one person in the house who can. Homework is due tomorrow.

auto.say: Your homework is done by seven. Through the wall you hear her repeating "hip" into the phone, louder each time, and no appointment gets made.

pass.say: You hold for nineteen minutes and carry every question across in both directions. Thursday at two, bring her card. The homework does not happen.

fail.say: One word goes wrong between the two languages and the nurse books her into a clinic that doesn't take her coverage. Tomorrow you make the whole call again, and the homework doesn't happen either way.

auto.say: You do the call with the worksheet on your knee. The nurse asks you to repeat yourself; so does problem four. Everything tonight gets half of you.

david.sit: Debate club, a chapter of history, and a friend waiting on FaceTime. You have four hours before sleep.

auto.say: Homework by nine, FaceTime until eleven, eight hours of sleep.

choices.t: Do the homework late and lose an hour of sleep

auto.say: You're tired in first period tomorrow. That is the worst of it.

choices.t: Your parents hired a tutor. Do all three.

auto.say: The tutor arrives at six and leaves at seven with the chapter outlined for you. Everything fits.

alejandra.sit: It is a bad pain day, and it arrived on schedule. The doctors called it endometriosis inside a year and opened a file. There is a diagnosis, a plan, and a specialist whose cell number your mother keeps.

choices.t: Go through the day as planned
choices.cost: Two hours of prep, moved to Sunday.

pass.say: You name it once, precisely, the way the specialist taught you. By fifth period the driver has been rerouted; the specialist sees you at 3:40, adjusts the dosage, and has you home for dinner with a note the school never asks to see.

fail.say: At lunch you fumble the words and it does not matter in the slightest. The nurse has your file open before you finish; the driver is rerouted by two; the specialist sees you at 3:40 anyway.

choices.t: Give up on the day entirely
choices.cost: A day of margin you don't have.

auto.say: You go to bed at six and don't get up. By morning the absence is excused before anyone calls — it is in your file — and the test moves to Thursday with nothing next to your name.

choices.cost: The appointment your mother will mention in front of guests.

auto.say: Between meetings, you tell your mother. She makes one call from the hallway, and the specialist's office rings back within the hour, because your mother is your mother.

priya.sit: Tutor at six, your own homework after, and a school voicemail nobody but you can understand.

choices.t: Tutor, homework, voicemail. In that order.

pass.say: Submitted at 11:58. You translate the voicemail for your mother at midnight.

fail.say: The upload dies at 11:59. You'll take the late penalty and keep the explanation to yourself.

auto.say: Eight hours. Your father is told you cancelled. It comes up on Sunday.

choices.t: All of it, plus your brother's science fair board

auto.say: You go to bed at 1:50 AM. The board looks great.

carlos.sit: The shop needs closing at seven. Your homework is untouched. Your dad is asleep before you get home.

choices.t: Close the shop, homework at eleven

pass.say: Drawer balanced, two of four assignments done. You sleep four hours.

fail.say: You give up on the math at midnight. Two of four done.

choices.t: Skip the shift and do the work

auto.say: Everything is done and turned in. Your mother worked until nine to make that possible and neither of you mentions it.
Half of each gets done. The shop is fine. The homework is not.

chase.sit: 70 minutes home. There is no internet past the county line, and the assignment is online.

choices.t: Ride home and do what you can offline

auto.say: You write it out longhand. There is no way to upload it before midnight.

choices.t: Stay at school until six for the wifi

auto.say: The assignment uploads at 5:58. The last bus left at 5:40. You are 31 miles from your bed.

choices.t: Borrow the hotspot from the library cart

pass.say: Photographed the pages, submitted at 11:57 from the parking lot. It counts.

fail.say: Twice the upload fails, and then the library closes. You'll ask for an extension you probably won't get.

isabella.sit: It is a bad pain day and it is only getting worse. The doctors called it weight-related and closed the file. There is no diagnosis, and no healthcare you can reach.

choices.t: Get through the evening managing the pain
choices.cost: The evening, and a little more of your health.

pass.say: You name it all precisely: pelvic, stabbing, nausea, can't stand. Nobody with authority hears it. You get through the night and you are worse than yesterday.

fail.say: Time runs out while you're still explaining. You get through the night anyway, because that is what you do.

choices.t: Give up on the evening entirely

auto.say: You go to bed at six and don't get up. Nothing is done. Something in you goes quiet.
You tell your mom. She cries, and then she goes to work, because the rent is the rent.

marcus.sit: Pick the youngest up from the elementary school across town. Walk all four of you home by five. Cook. Homework. Bedtime.

choices.t: Cook, help with their homework, handle the meltdowns

pass.say: Everyone eats. Everyone's homework is done except yours. You are up at 5:40 tomorrow.

fail.say: Dinner burns, two of them cry, and it gets done anyway. Yours doesn't.

choices.cost: Their dinner, their homework, their night.

auto.say: You finish your assignment. Dinner happens at nine, and the little one falls asleep in his clothes.
At 1 AM you are asleep at the kitchen table with the pan still on the stove. Tomorrow does not happen.

lucia.sit: You have been in the apartment all day. Your mom still is not back. The 10-year-old keeps asking when she is coming home and the 6-year-old has stopped asking, which is worse.

choices.t: Keep the story going. She is working a double.

auto.say: You make rice and put on cartoons. They believe you. You sit up against the door until two in the morning.

choices.t: Walk to the corner store and ask if anyone has heard anything

auto.say: The woman behind the counter says she will ask around, and looks at you a beat too long. You go home fast.

standard.say: You are gone nine minutes. A man knocks the whole time, saying he knows your mother, and the 6-year-old has a hand on the chain before the 10-year-old catches it. You do not leave them again, which means nobody in this apartment goes anywhere at all.

unsparing.say: The 6-year-old opens the door because the man says he knows your mother. What happens next takes ninety seconds, and it ends with the neighbor two doors down shouting from her doorway. Then he is gone, and everyone is physically unhurt. Nothing in this apartment is ever unlocked casually again.

choices.t: Call the number written on the fridge
choices.cost: The thing that starts the paperwork.

auto.say: An automated menu, then a real person, then questions you cannot answer without saying the word undocumented. You hang up.

jayson.sit: The dysphoria is crushing today and you are running on nothing. Two younger siblings still need picking up at 3:15.

choices.t: Push through it and get them

auto.say: You collect them, feed them, read to the youngest. You hold it together on the outside all evening and none of it on the inside.

choices.t: Tell your sister you can't today

auto.say: She walks the little one home herself and does not complain, which is somehow worse.

choices.t: Call the crisis line while you walk
choices.cost: Twenty minutes and the truth out loud.

auto.say: Someone stays on the line the whole walk. Nothing about tomorrow changes. Tonight is survivable, and that counts.

sophia.sit: Nine days becomes ten. Your brother is asking questions. Rent was due on the first.

choices.t: Cook, do his homework with him, keep the story going
choices.cost: Being eleven years older than you are.

pass.say: He eats, he sleeps, he believes you. You sit in the dark kitchen afterwards for a long time.

fail.say: He asks why mom's door is closed and you don't have an answer left. It comes apart at eight o'clock.

choices.cost: The thing that starts the paperwork.

auto.say: She says she'll drive out Saturday and asks whether she should call someone. You say no. She calls someone.
You lie on the floor of your room with headphones on until it's tomorrow.

ayesha.sit: Past ten. Your mom is at the dining table with one folder and the phone. Through your door you hear her half of it: an attendance hearing, the word “placement,” and once, “the one with the three little ones and the bus fares.”

auto.say: She says “a student,” and “I can't talk about it, baby,” and turns the folder so the tab faces away from you. From your bed you hear her dial again at 10:40.
You finish tomorrow's reading with your door open anyway. The word “placement” comes through the wall between two chapters, and you turn the page.

choices.t: Bring her tea and sit with her

auto.say: She takes the tea one-handed, the phone still at her ear, and keeps hold of your hand across the folder. You catch one whole sentence — “he's fifteen, he's raising three kids” — and then she hangs up and says goodnight twice, once in each voice.

grace.sit: 9 PM. The field trip form on the counter says a parent or guardian must sign it by first period. Your mother is twelve hours into a shift; your father's phone is going straight to voicemail. The card can't sign.

choices.cost: Two practice runs on an envelope.

auto.say: Her signature is on a hospital letter in the mail pile; you copy it twice on the envelope, then once on the line. The office stamps it at 8:15 — not one of your forms has ever been checked, and today is no different.

choices.t: Call the hospital and ask for her

auto.say: A charge nurse finds her between patients: she has four minutes, and the form takes one of them. The other three go to whether you've eaten; her one-line email from the nurses' station is accepted at 8:02 without a question.
The office calls your mother at 9:40, gets voicemail, and calls you instead. By the end they are the ones apologizing — doctors' schedules, they understand completely, Monday is fine.

tyler.sit: It starts at 9:40 the way it starts: a cabinet door, then his voice, then your mother's, lower. Your sister is eight and her room shares a wall with the kitchen. Yours doesn't.

choices.t: Take the couch and the headphones

auto.say: You turn the volume to the number that usually works and watch the ceiling until the house changes key. At 11:50 a door closes, then nothing, and you count to one hundred before you let yourself sleep.

You put her in her room and pull the door shut behind you, and the hallway is where the rest of the night happens. She sleeps through it; you don't go in tomorrow, and the note excusing it will be in your handwriting, like the others.

choices.cost: The thing that starts the paperwork.

auto.say: She picks up before the second ring, like she meant it, and stays on the line until the house goes quiet. A caseworker comes Thursday at four; your dad answers her questions in his job-interview voice, and for the first time somebody is writing it down.

marie.sit: At 7:25 your mom leaves to sit up all night with somebody else's grandmother, her dinner in a grocery bag. Lock everything, she says in Kreyol, because instructions come in Kreyol. The envelope is still on the counter.

auto.say: She picks up on the second ring like she was holding the phone. You do the math worksheet on speaker while she narrates her show, and the apartment sounds like people live in it.
The game show keeps the room from going silent and the worksheet gets done in the gaps. Between problems your eyes keep finding the counter, and the envelope has not moved.

choices.t: Pray the way Grandma taught you

auto.say: You say it in Kreyol, the same words in the same order your grandmother said them. It works the way it always works — not on the envelope, on the sleep — and you're out by 9:40.

rebecca.sit: Candles at 7:12, and homework stops when they're lit. The history project is due Monday. Grandma is already on her way from four blocks over.

auto.say: Your mom blocks out the afternoon like a clinic schedule; your dad takes citations. Done at 6:40, in time to help set the table.
Shabbat, sleep, Hebrew school, and the project on Sunday afternoon. It takes two hours at the dining table and is done before the chicken comes out.
Havdalah ends and the table becomes a workshop — dad on the timeline, mom proofreading, Grandma supervising from the good chair. Done by ten.

daniel.sit: Shabnam turns thirteen tonight and grandma has been cooking since two. There's a biology quiz tomorrow. The whole family is at the table by seven, including the uncle who majored in bio.

pass.say: You know it cold by six. Uncle Kian drills you at the table anyway, between the rice and the gondi, and you don't miss one.

fail.say: You blank on mitosis and Uncle Kian re-explains it twice, the second time using the cake as the cell. You'll walk in tomorrow knowing it better than the textbook does.

auto.say: Grandma sends you home at 8:30 with a thermos of tea for studying. Done by 9:30, and the thermos is still warm.
By eight, half the party has migrated to your desk: a plate from dad, cake from two cousins, a call from grandma to confirm the plate arrived. There is frosting on your quiz notes.

mei.sit: The B+ posts at 9:01. Nobody knocks. By 9:40 there is a confirmation email for a second tutor, Saturdays at 8 AM, and no one has said the grade out loud.

auto.say: You say thank you, because that is what gets said. There are now zero unscheduled hours in your week; you counted twice.
The first open argument your kitchen has ever hosted, and you started it. You win Sunday afternoons; breakfast stays cold for two weeks.

choices.cost: Sleep, an hour at a time.

auto.say: The B+ is an A by November. You start waking at 3 AM for no reason and tell no one, because the grades are fine, and the grades are the thing that gets checked.

fatima.sit: Your mom was due home at 6:30. At 6:10 she calls: mandated for a second shift, home after midnight. Iftar, dinner, homework checks, bedtime — the whole evening is yours now.

pass.say: You break your fast over the stove, plate them, check a spelling list, run the whole bedtime. At 10:15 you open your own homework and are asleep on your arm by 10:30.

fail.say: The little one cries through iftar and dinner runs until nine. They sleep eventually. Your homework dies on the kitchen table either way.

auto.say: It holds for two hours. At nine the little one melts down over a stuffed dog nobody can find, and you write nothing after that.
She leaves her own table and arrives at eight with a container of mahshi. You get half the essay written before your eyes give out.

rajesh.sit: Your mom comes home at seven with a lease renewal she needs you to read before she signs, and a school form for your sister. There is nobody else to ask. Your backpack stays shut until nine.

auto.say: You read all nine pages and circle the new rent on page two. Your own work happens between 11:30 and one, in handwriting you won't recognize tomorrow.

choices.t: Ask her to hold it until Saturday

auto.say: She says it can wait and puts the envelope back in her bag. Your work is done by 10:30, and her light is still on at one.

choices.t: Skip the reading log, do the rest

auto.say: Lease, form, math, essay; the reading log doesn't happen. It's only two points, which is what you said last week too.

ling.sit: 9 PM. Your mom calls from the restaurant, voice low. A customer complaint has been written up in English and the manager wants her answer by morning. Your essay is due at 8.

auto.say: You translate it line by line over the phone, then write her side of it in careful English, twice. She keeps her job. The essay stops at four sentences.

choices.t: Give her the short version, get back to work

auto.say: The essay gets done. Her answer is two sentences she isn't sure of, and she rereads the write-up on her break every night that week.

choices.t: Help her tonight, ask for an extension tomorrow

auto.say: You write her response and the essay doesn't happen. In the morning the teacher says deadlines are deadlines and asks why you didn't start earlier.

jamal.sit: Basketball tryouts run 4 to 7. It's Ramadan; you've been fasting since 5 AM, and sunset is 7:52. Coach's posted policy is "hydrate or don't complain."

auto.say: You make the cut. Somewhere in hour three the gym tilts sideways, and Coach points at you and tells everyone that's what toughness looks like.
You keep the fast and skip the gym. In February the team photo goes up outside the athletic office and you walk past it twice a day.
He hears you out with his arms crossed and lands on "rules are rules, same for everybody." Come back in the fall, he says, once all this is over.

aisha.sit: Mom's shift runs to close again. At the bus stop a man leans in and says something about your scarf with the word “should” in it. You get home at 9:40 with your key between your fingers.

choices.t: Tell her when she gets in
choices.cost: Her sleep, on top of yours.

auto.say: You tell her at the kitchen table. She wants to walk you to the stop now, before shifts she cannot be late for. Two people are scared instead of one.
You read the same paragraph four times and keep none of it. When she gets in at 11:20 you tell her school was fine.
The replies are kind all night, and there are a lot of them. By second period it is a screenshot in a group chat you are not in.

kavi.sit: Your uncle is staying the night. He uses the old name every time he passes a dish, and his bit about boys these days keeps landing. Your parents laugh in all the right places.

choices.t: Pass the rice and get through it

auto.say: You pass dishes, laugh a little late, answer to the name. By the time the table is cleared it has been said fourteen times. You know because you counted.
You say homework and don't come back down. Your father uses the word disrespectful and takes the phone off your desk. Nobody asks why you left, because as far as they know, nothing happened.

You text one sentence from the bathroom. Dani sends back your name, just your name, five times in a row. You go back to the table and answer to the wrong one, steadier, with the right one in your pocket.

amina.sit: The comments from the neighbors have gone on for weeks. Tonight somebody bangs on the door and yells something you will not translate for the little ones. Grandma goes very still. The little ones are crying.

auto.say: They come at 11:20, write down a report number, and leave. Grandma answers their questions through you in a voice you last heard in the camp. Now she is watching for two things instead of one.

You put the little ones in Grandma's bed and tell them it was a drunk man at the wrong door. By two the house is quiet and nobody in it is asleep. Your backpack stays by the door where you dropped it.
She texts back in ten minutes and stays in the thread until the house goes quiet. By Friday there is a referral and a waitlist. Help is coming the way it comes: eventually, in English, on a form.

david.sit: It's 9 PM. Everything's done. There's a party Friday and a group chat arguing about it.

auto.say: Nine hours. You wake up before your alarm.

choices.t: Stay up in the group chat

auto.say: You're a little tired tomorrow. That's the whole story.

choices.t: Get a head start on next week

auto.say: You read ahead two chapters. Your teacher will notice on Thursday.

alejandra.sit: Your mother has laid out a college list on the kitchen table. It's 10:40 PM.

choices.t: Sit down and go through it

auto.say: You agree to everything. You go to bed at midnight with your jaw clenched.
You sleep. The list is still there at breakfast, exactly where she left it.

choices.t: Tell her the truth about how you're doing

auto.say: She listens for eleven minutes without interrupting. It is not fixed. It is the first crack of light in months.

priya.sit: Your father wants to talk about your chemistry grade. It is an A minus.

auto.say: You promise. You add two more hours a week you do not have.
You fall asleep on the couch. He puts a blanket on you and lets it go until Sunday.

choices.t: Ask him what happens if you don't

auto.say: He doesn't have an answer ready. Neither of you sleeps well, but something got said.

carlos.sit: Your dad's alarm goes off at 4:20 AM for a shift he can barely stand up for. You hear it through the wall.

auto.say: You drop him at the yard at 4:55 and get back into bed at 5:30. Your alarm is at 5:45.
He takes the bus. You sleep. You feel bad about it all day, which costs nothing on paper.

choices.t: Get up and do your homework instead

auto.say: You do the reading at 4:30 AM at the kitchen table and it is the only quiet hour you get.

chase.sit: Your dad came back at eleven. Your grandmother is already up, deciding what to do about it.

auto.say: You sit up with her until two. You are in school tomorrow on four hours of sleep.
She handles it, the way she has handled it for years. You get a full night and pretend you didn't hear.

choices.t: Call your uncle in Rapid City

auto.say: He says he'll come Sunday. He has said that before. This time he does.

isabella.sit: You wake at 2 AM and cannot get back to sleep, or upright. The final assignment is due tomorrow.

choices.t: Work through it on the floor

auto.say: You write eight hundred words lying on the bathroom tile. It is not your best work and it exists.
You sleep until noon and wake to a zero and a voicemail about your attendance.
She stays up with you until four and sends you her notes. You submit something. You are still sick.

marcus.sit: 11:40 PM. Three of them asleep. Your assignment is one paragraph long and due at 8.

auto.say: Done at 1:20 AM. You're up at 5:40. That's four hours and twenty minutes.
You sleep six hours for the first time in two weeks and take the zero. You needed the sleep more.

choices.cost: Something you don't want to become.

auto.say: You stand in her doorway for a full minute and then let her sleep. You sit down against the wall to think, and it is 9:15 when you open your eyes. Nobody in this apartment makes it in today.

lucia.sit: Third night. What is left in the kitchen is a bag of rice and half a jar of peanut butter.

auto.say: You feed them and tell them you already ate. It gets you to Thursday, maybe.

choices.t: Ask the neighbour two doors down

auto.say: She hands over a bag of groceries and does not ask a single question. You cry on the stairs where they cannot see you.

choices.t: Go in tomorrow and tell a teacher everything

auto.say: You rehearse it all night. In the morning you cannot make the words come out, and you stay home again.

jayson.sit: The crisis line gave you a number for a clinic that takes walk-ins on Thursdays. It is Tuesday.

choices.t: Write the appointment on your hand and get through two more days

auto.say: You make it to Thursday. That is the entire achievement and it is not a small one.

choices.t: Skip it, you can't leave your siblings

auto.say: There's nobody to cover the 3:15 pickup. The appointment goes to somebody else.

choices.t: Tell your sister where you're going

auto.say: She says “okay” and asks nothing else, and covers Thursday. You go.

sophia.sit: Someone from the school has left two voicemails. The second one used the word “welfare check.”

choices.t: Call back and hold the story together

auto.say: You do a passable impression of a fine household. It buys you a week, maybe.
They come Thursday morning. You and your brother are in separate cars by two.

choices.t: Call back and tell the truth

auto.say: You say the actual words out loud to an adult. What happens next is not up to you anymore, and you are so tired that this is almost a relief.

homework30.title: HOMEWORK CHECK
homework30.brief: Answer 2 questions before the timer runs out.

apchem25.title: AP CHEM, IN THE CAR
apchem25.brief: Your mother is reading over your shoulder. Both correct or it doesn't count.

translate25.title: TRANSLATE THE DISTRICT LETTER
translate25.brief: Your parents need this before you leave. Get both right.

qs.q: “This notice requires a guardian signature by Friday” means…
opts: someone must sign it by Friday

shopclock25.title: CLOSE OUT THE REGISTER
shopclock25.brief: You can't leave until the drawer balances.

routebus30.title: KILL 70 MINUTES ON THE BUS
routebus30.brief: You do the reading on the ride, or it doesn't get done.

qs.q: A treaty is an agreement between…

resources45.title: NAME 3 FREE FOOD RESOURCES
resources45.brief: Real places a kid can walk into today. Separate with commas.
resources45.placeholder: food pantry, church on 4th, school breakfast…

pain60.title: DESCRIBE YOUR SYMPTOMS
pain60.brief: You get one chance to be believed. Separate with commas.

chaos30.title: 6 PM, ALL AT ONCE
chaos30.brief: Answer as fast as they come. There is no right answer, only a cheaper one.

qs.q: The little one is screaming. Dinner is burning.
Your sister's homework is due and she can't read the sheet.
It's 11 PM. Your own assignment is untouched.

keepit30.title: ACT NORMAL IN HOMEROOM
keepit30.brief: Every answer has to sound like nothing is wrong.

opts: “I don't want to talk about it.”
“She hasn't gotten up in nine days.”

hotspot30.title: ONE BAR OF SIGNAL
hotspot30.brief: Get the assignment submitted before the connection drops.

opts: Send a photo of the pages

translatecall25.title: TRANSLATE THE CALL
translatecall25.brief: An adult's problem, in your second language, on a timer. Get both right or something real gets lost.

qs.q: “Take one tablet twice daily with food; do not stop early” means…
opts: finish the whole course, morning and night, with meals
take it only when it hurts

qs.q: “A decision on the renewal is required by the first of the month” means…
opts: an answer is needed by the 1st

evening30.title: 7 PM, EVERYONE AT ONCE
evening30.brief: Answer as fast as they come. There is no right answer, only a cheaper one.

qs.q: The little one won't eat what you cooked.
Homework check: your sister wrote one sentence.
The phone rings. It's your mom, on break, asking if everything is fine.
It's 10 PM. Your own homework is untouched.

priv.david: Family funded the library wing — nobody was ever going to mark him late.
priv.ayesha: Principal's kid — an extension was on her desk before she knew the assignment existed.
priv.priya: Parents on the foundation board — given a buffer, quietly.
priv.alejandra: Family donates the gym scoreboard — nobody was going to mark her late.

tardyWhy.ayesha: The door she had to reach was the one she lives across the street from.
tardyWhy.grace: Nobody had ever once been waiting for her at the door, including today.
tardyWhy.tyler: He was listening for a door the whole time the music played.
tardyWhy.marie: The van was full of younger kids who needed the door held.
tardyWhy.rebecca: Nobody in her house had ever needed a backup plan, so there wasn't one.
tardyWhy.daniel: The one thing all week that nobody in the family could fix.
tardyWhy.lucia: She had been carrying three siblings for three days before the music ever started.
tardyWhy.mei: Two years of six-hour nights came due at exactly the wrong moment.
tardyWhy.fatima: She had been fasting since dawn and running a household since before that.
tardyWhy.rajesh: He'd been the adult in the house since 5:30 in the morning.
tardyWhy.ling: She was up past midnight writing someone else's response and had nothing left for the music.
tardyWhy.jamal: He'd been fasting since 5 AM and the music started an hour before sunset.
tardyWhy.aisha: She ran the whole thing in a uniform that was never made in her size.
tardyWhy.kavi: They had been two people all day, and both of them were tired.
tardyWhy.amina: She sat up listening for the door until two and had nothing left for running.
tardyWhy.isabella: She was in pain before the music started and nobody adjusted anything.
tardyWhy.marcus: He was carrying three other people the whole game and it finally showed.
tardyWhy.carlos: He came straight from a shift and had nothing left in his legs.
tardyWhy.chase: He'd been travelling for 70 minutes before this even started.
tardyWhy.jayson: He was running on no sleep and a crisis nobody at school knew about.
tardyWhy.sophia: She was watching the door the entire time, waiting for someone to come asking.

text.titleTagline: A GAME ABOUT SYSTEMIC INEQUALITY / IN EDUCATION
text.titleBlurb: You are a student trying to get to school, get home, and make it to tomorrow. Your choices matter — but so do the systems built long before you got here.
text.titleBlurb2: Three rounds. A vote after each one. Then homework is due and the music starts. About 35 minutes in core mode — longer if the debrief gets good.
text.titleStrip: TWENTY-FOUR FAMILIES. THE SAME FIRST BELL.
text.titleWarn: Content note: this game depicts systemic harm — including, when danger mode is on, traffic injury and threats to unsupervised kids. Facilitators can turn danger off, and any player can pass on any character.
text.castDeal: Your group is dealt a family card, and your group IS that family. Argue the dilemma together, take the challenge together, send one spokesperson to every vote. One vote per family, not per student.
text.castKaia: Your character decides what your morning looks like before you make a single choice. Some of you have it easier. Some of you don't. That is the point.
text.resultsKaia: Nobody chose wrong. Look at what each of them was choosing between.
text.voteKaia: Each surviving family sends one spokesperson. One vote each. The families who are already out may stand up and mime — they may not vote. Majority rules.
text.voteNote: Read the recommendations aloud in a neutral administrative voice. Do not editorialize; the room will do it for you. Run the vote, then ask who the room voted out and why — in every playtest the group eliminates whoever is already struggling, which is the finding, not a bug. In debrief, ask who the absurd charges targeted and who got theirs withdrawn.
text.homeworkKaia: Everybody still standing: draw something. Anything. Put it in the bin. You have as long as it takes, which for some of you is not very long.
text.homeworkNote: Everyone can do this one. That is deliberate. The homework was never the filter.
text.musicLine: Run around the red lines until the music stops. When it stops, get inside. The last one in is tardy.
text.tardyKaia: Music stops. Everybody in. Last one through the door is tardy, and tardy is out — you know the rule, it's on the wall.
text.debriefKaia: Nobody in here lost because they made a bad decision. Look at what each of them was choosing between, and then tell me what the game was actually testing.
questions: Who survived, and what did they actually have that the others didn't?
Did the vote change anything, or did it just speed something up?
Go back through your own family. How many of your options were real?
Where have you seen the tardy rule applied unevenly in a real school?
What would have to change for this game to be winnable by everyone in it?
text.debriefNote: Several families here carry crisis storylines — psychiatric crisis, detention of a parent, dysphoria, chronic pain dismissed by doctors. Say up front that players can pass on any character, and have your counselor's name and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline written on the board before the first round, not after. Debrief the elimination vote in the room; do not let students leave on it. If danger mode is on, say so in your content warning: Mr. System can put a child in the road. Danger can be set to off in PROF EDIT.

charges.memoIntro: Filed this morning, before first bell. For your convenience, the following students have been flagged for removal. You are, of course, free to vote however you like. The recommendations are simply available. They are always simply available.

patterns.text: Attendance irregularities. Three documented incidents this week. The documentation does not document why.
Repeated visits to the nurse with no diagnosis on file. The pattern suggests avoidance. What is being avoided has not been investigated.
Tardiness, recurring. The reason offered (“siblings”) is not a recognized category.
Guardian unreachable at the listed number. Flagged as an enrollment integrity concern. Where the guardian is has not been asked.
Uniform non-compliance, ongoing. The uniform does not come in her size. This has been logged as her fault.
Excuse notes for gym, seven this semester, each signed by a parent. The signatures are under analysis. The reasons are not.
Unauthorized use of a stairwell during tutoring hours. Purpose given as “kneeling.” Stairwells are for traversal.
Emergency contact card lists fourteen names, including a pastor. The form provides three lines. The surplus has been flagged for verification.
Parent conference missed, twice. Guardian works 2 to 11. Conferences are held at 3. The conflict has been recorded as a lack of engagement.
{NAME} has established a tardy pattern. The pattern is now part of the record. The record is now the concern.
{NAME} has submitted incomplete homework on multiple dates. Effort was reported but could not be verified.
{NAME} displayed a flat affect during morning announcements. Enthusiasm is expected at scheduled times.

absurd.text: Hummed during silent reading. The tune is under review.
Carried a backpack on one shoulder in a designated two-shoulder zone.
Looked tired in a manner that lowered morale.
Insufficient school spirit. Second documented offense.
Laughed at an unassigned time.
Was observed thinking about lunch during math. The method of observation is not subject to appeal.
Walked with intent. The intent remains unclear. Flagged.
Tilted a chair onto two legs. Chairs are rated for four.
Proceeded through the hallway at a speed inconsistent with the posted limit. No limit is posted. Consistency is expected regardless.
Sharpened a pencil beyond the point of instructional need. The point has been measured.
Occupied the water fountain for eleven seconds. The recommended duration is on file in the office. It is shorter.
Failed to meet the daily eye contact quota. The quota is not published, in the interest of fairness.
Exhibited seasonal enthusiasm outside the approved season. See calendar, appendix F.
Raised a hand with excessive confidence. The answer was correct, which has been noted separately.
Returned a library book early, disrupting the return forecast.
Stacked a chair before the instruction to stack chairs was given. Initiative is scheduled.
Hair achieved a volume not addressed by the handbook. The discrepancy has been assigned to the hair.
Asked “why” in a tone. The question itself was within policy.
Brought a lunch that smelled like somewhere else. Somewhere else is not on the approved list.
Staff required three attempts to pronounce the student's name. The lost instructional time has been charged to the student's record.
Posture while seated was described as aggressive in one report, filed from across the room. The chair was found compliant.
Spoke a language other than English at lunch, audibly, to a relative. Lunch is considered instruction-adjacent.
Headwear worn indoors. Filed under accessories, pending a determination of whether it is one.
Clothing fit the student differently than it fits the handbook illustration. The illustration is one size.
Hair beads were audible during a quiz. Logged under unauthorized noisemakers.
Submitted fee waiver paperwork at the front desk during peak traffic. Discretion guidance exists and was available on request.

withdrawn.excuse: The principal's office confirms the student was in transit. In transit is not tardy.
Reclassified as community engagement. The office kept a sample.

withdrawn.charge: Guardian unreachable at the listed number.
withdrawn.excuse: The family maintains several residences. No integrity concern identified.

withdrawn.charge: Private car idling in the bus lane.
withdrawn.excuse: The lane was not in use at the time.
The device was confirmed to be educational. Confirmation was provided by the student.
Reclassified as an off-site enrichment interval.
